claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed primarily by formation of a stable, self-healing oxide film.
Increasing chromium or molybdenum concentration promotes formation of a stable, self-healing oxide film.
The oxide film passivates the surface and reduces metal-ion dissolution.
Strong adhesion of the oxide film to the substrate diminishes wear-induced film removal.
Chromium and molybdenum are passive elements that form protective oxides in HEAs.
Increasing chromium or molybdenum content relative to a baseline HEA will produce a more continuous oxide film.
Increasing chromium or molybdenum content relative to a baseline HEA will produce a more adherent oxide film.
Increasing chromium or molybdenum content relative to a baseline HEA will produce a more self-healing oxide film.
The relevant structural mediator can be a Cr2O3- or spinel-based surface film.
The superior oxide film prevents further oxidation by passivating the surface.
The superior oxide film resists mechanical fragmentation and thereby lowers wear.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, enhanced passive-element content will produce a more robust oxide film than the baseline composition.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, enhanced passive-element content will reduce wear volume relative to the baseline alloy.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, enhanced passive-element content will reduce corrosion current density relative to the baseline alloy.
The baseline HEA forms a less protective oxide film and consequently exhibits higher wear and corrosion rates.
The predicted benefit requires sufficient oxygen for oxide-film formation.
The predicted benefit requires mechanical loads below the oxide film's adhesion-strength limit.
The prediction may fail in oxygen-deprived environments.
The prediction may fail under extreme abrasion that continually disrupts the protective film.
